layers.name: Ways of reading
layers.description: How people take this passage: as history, origin story, symbol, worship… Where readers disagree, every reading is shown with who holds it.

categories.label: exalted prose
categories.about: Exalted prose: elevated, patterned prose between narrative and poetry (a proposed reading of Genesis 1).
categories.implications: Reading as exalted prose emphasises pattern and liturgy over chronology.

categories.label: cosmology and polemic
categories.about: Ancient Near Eastern cosmology and polemic: a creation account answering neighbouring myths.
categories.implications: This reading asks what the text affirms against rival views of the gods and the world.

categories.label: temple inauguration
categories.about: Temple inauguration: creation read as God dedicating the cosmos as a temple (proposed by John Walton).
categories.implications: This reading stresses function and God taking up residence rather than material origins.

categories.label: ancient biography
categories.about: Ancient biography (bios).
categories.implications: Ancient lives selected and arranged material to show character, unlike modern biography.

categories.label: scripture-shaped retelling
categories.about: Scripture-shaped retelling.
categories.implications: Read alongside the earlier scriptures it uses.

categories.label: type-scene
categories.about: A type-scene or patterned story (e.g. annunciation, the Moses pattern).
categories.implications: Readers compare it with other examples to see what is distinctive.

categories.label: eyewitness testimony
categories.about: Eyewitness testimony.
categories.implications: Read as resting on named witnesses.

categories.label: visionary / symbolic
categories.about: Vision account.
categories.implications: Read as describing visionary experience.

categories.label: told as history
categories.about: Presents itself as an account of past events: historical report, theological history, schematic history, annal.
categories.implications: Readers ask what happened and why the writer tells it this way. Readings differ on how far selection, theology and schemes (ages, round numbers) shape the account.

categories.label: origin story or myth
categories.about: Myth in the scholarly sense: stories that found a people’s identity, world-order and practices. Includes founding myth, cosmogony, primeval history and etiology.
categories.implications: Reading a passage as founding myth asks what it establishes about God, humanity and Israel. It does not by itself mean the passage is untrue; many hold this together with historical or theological truth-claims.

categories.label: answering other beliefs
categories.about: A passage that answers or rewrites a rival story, such as Genesis 1 alongside Mesopotamian creation accounts.
categories.implications: Readers notice what is denied or reversed, for example the sun and moon made as mere lamps rather than gods.

categories.label: hero story or legend
categories.about: Stories of ancestors, deliverers and tricksters: hero tale, ancestral saga, legend, folk tale (cf. Gunkel’s Sagen).
categories.implications: Readers attend to type-scenes, character and moral ambiguity, and how a people’s story is told through individuals. Heroes are often flawed.

categories.label: humour and irony
categories.about: Humour, irony, satire and comic reversal, such as Jonah’s reluctant prophet, Esther’s reversals or Balaam’s donkey.
categories.implications: Humour carries meaning. Readers ask who is being laughed at and why. Comic does not mean trivial.

categories.label: symbol and figure
categories.about: Meaning carried by images and patterns: figurative, symbolic, allegorical, parabolic, typological.
categories.implications: Readers follow the images rather than a plain sequence of events. "Figurative (metaphor-rich)" is found by a rule from the density of metaphors.

categories.label: vision
categories.about: Revealed, symbolic portrayals of heavenly realities or the end: visionary, apocalyptic, prophetic vision.
categories.implications: Images are decoded rather than read as plain narrative. Numbers, beasts and colours are usually symbolic.

categories.label: worship and teaching
categories.about: Text shaped for worship, teaching or reflection: hymnic, instruction (torah), exemplary tale, wisdom reflection.
categories.implications: Readers ask how the text was used, in worship or teaching, as well as what it says.

categories.label: retelling earlier scripture
categories.about: Composed from earlier scripture: midrashic retelling, prophecy historicised, intertextual retelling.
categories.implications: Readers trace the source texts and notice what the retelling changes.

layers.about: How people take this passage: as history, origin story, symbol, worship… Where readers disagree, every reading is shown with who holds it.
layers.implications: Reading a passage as history, as an origin story or as worship changes the questions you ask of it and what counts as its truth. Where readers disagree, every reading is shown with who holds it, and none is ranked.

cosmology and polemic: ancient Near Eastern cosmology and polemic

ai_suggest.instruction: Identify how passages speak about reality (history, origin story, worship, symbol and so on). Use the exact mode terms from the vocabulary, grouped by family. Where published scholars disagree, give each reading as a separate contested option with the same contested_group, naming its proponent (author, title, year). Always include more than one reading where scholars differ; never rank them.

layers.name: Intertext

categories.label: cross-reference
categories.about: A cross-reference that readers have found helpful (OpenBible votes).
categories.implications: Follow it to compare wording and context.

layers.about: Other passages this one quotes, echoes or is commonly linked with.
layers.implications: Scripture often interprets scripture. Following a link can show where an image or phrase comes from and how its meaning grows or shifts.

layers.name: Typology

categories.label: type
categories.about: A proposed type–antitype link.
categories.implications: An interpretive link, not a statement in the text itself.

ai_suggest.instruction: Identify type-antitype links that published interpreters propose, naming them.

layers.about: Links where a person, event or institution is read as foreshadowing a later one (type and antitype).
layers.implications: Typology is an interpretive move, mainly Christian. Seeing a link as typology says something about how the two passages are read together, not only about each passage on its own.
layers.caution: Typology is an interpretive reading, mainly Christian, not a statement in the text itself.

layers.name: Reception

categories.label: tradition
categories.about: A reading from the history of interpretation.
categories.implications: Shows how one tradition understood the passage.

layers.about: How the passage has been read, preached, sung and pictured through history.
layers.implications: Shows that readings have a history: the same words have meant different things to different communities. It helps separate what the text says from what later tradition made of it.

layers.name: Historical setting
layers.description: Authorship, date and dated events (unfoldingWord; Theographic traditional chronology)

categories.label: context
categories.about: Book-level setting: authorship and date.
categories.implications: Often debated; read with the alternatives in mind.

categories.label: dated event
categories.about: A dated event (Theographic traditional chronology).
categories.implications: Dates follow one traditional system; others differ.

layers.about: Setting, authorship, dating and dated events.
layers.implications: When and by whom a text was written shapes what it would have meant to its first hearers. Dates and authorship are often debated; the chronology shown is one traditional system.

layers.name: Places

categories.label: site
categories.about: A place named in the text and its likely location.
categories.implications: Disputed identifications are shown as equal options.

layers.about: Places named in the passage, with their likely locations.
layers.implications: Geography carries meaning: journeys, borders and sacred sites. Some identifications are certain, others are disputed and shown as equal options.

layers.name: Nature

categories.label: species
categories.about: A living thing in the text.
categories.implications: Picture the real creature or plant.

categories.label: animals
categories.about: Animals mentioned.
categories.implications: Often figurative as well as literal.

categories.label: plants
categories.about: Plants mentioned.
categories.implications: Vines, figs and olives often stand for Israel or blessing.

categories.label: weather
categories.about: Weather mentioned.
categories.implications: Storms and rain often signal God’s presence or judgement.

categories.label: land and water
categories.about: Land and water mentioned.
categories.implications: Mountains, seas and wilderness carry symbolic weight.

categories.label: sky
categories.about: Sun, moon, stars and heavens.
categories.implications: Cosmic language, often used in creation and judgement texts.

layers.about: Animals, plants, weather, land, water and sky mentioned in the passage.
layers.implications: Biblical writers draw heavily on the natural world, often figuratively. Knowing the real creature or plant helps a reader feel an image as first hearers did.

layers.name: Objects & daily life

categories.label: object
categories.about: An everyday object.
categories.implications: Objects carry social and symbolic meaning.

categories.label: food and drink
categories.about: Food and drink.
categories.implications: Meals mark covenant, welcome and celebration.

categories.label: clothing
categories.about: Clothing.
categories.implications: Garments signal status, mourning or office.

categories.label: buildings
categories.about: Buildings and structures.
categories.implications: Gates, walls and the temple carry civic and sacred meaning.

categories.label: tools and weapons
categories.about: Tools and weapons.
categories.implications: Often used figuratively (sword of the mouth, ploughshares).

categories.label: money and measures
categories.about: Money and measures.
categories.implications: Values and sizes help picture the scene.

categories.label: vessels
categories.about: Vessels.
categories.implications: Cups and bowls often carry symbolic weight (the cup of wrath).

layers.about: Food, clothing, buildings, tools, money, measures and vessels mentioned in the passage.
layers.implications: Everyday objects carry social meaning, such as status, ritual purity or poverty. They help a reader picture the scene and notice symbolic uses.

layers.name: Archaeology

categories.label: evidence
categories.about: Material evidence connected with the passage.
categories.implications: Evidence quality varies and is labelled.

layers.about: Material evidence connected with places and practices in the passage.
layers.implications: Archaeology can illuminate daily life and settings, but rarely proves or disproves a story by itself. Evidence quality varies and is labelled.

layers.name: Form (story, poem, law…)
layers.description: The shape you can see in the text: a family tree, a lament, a parable, a law… Coloured by family (narrative, poetry, law…), labelled with the exact shape.

categories.label: narrative
categories.about: A narrative form: genealogy, call narrative, theophany, miracle story, parable, sermon, passion or resurrection account, etiological note.
categories.implications: Each form has conventions; departures from them are often the point.

categories.label: law
categories.about: A legal form: apodictic law ("You shall not…"), case law ("If a man…") or ritual instruction.
categories.implications: Absolute commands set boundaries; case laws work through examples. Reading a law with its form helps avoid over-generalising it.

categories.label: poetry
categories.about: A poetic form: hymn, lament, thanksgiving, royal or wisdom psalm, love song (psalm types after Gunkel; scholars differ).
categories.implications: A lament moves from complaint to trust; a hymn from call to praise to reasons. Knowing the type shows the shape of the prayer.

categories.label: wisdom
categories.about: A wisdom form: proverb or wisdom dialogue.
categories.implications: Proverbs state what is generally true, not promises. Dialogues such as Job test easy answers.

categories.label: prophecy
categories.about: A prophetic form: judgement, woe or salvation oracle, vision report, symbolic act.
categories.implications: Oracles follow patterns (accusation, then announcement). Symbolic acts are enacted messages.

categories.label: apocalyptic
categories.about: Apocalyptic writing: revealed visions of heavenly realities and the end, told in symbols (Daniel 7–12, Revelation, Mark 13, Matthew 24).
categories.implications: Apocalyptic images are read as symbols to decode, not as plain description.

categories.label: letter
categories.about: A letter form: opening and greeting, thanksgiving, household code, vice or virtue list, closing benediction.
categories.implications: Ancient letters had standard parts; changes to them signal emphasis.

ai_suggest.instruction: Identify passages that match a form in the vocabulary. Label each tag with the exact vocabulary term.

layers.about: The shape you can see in the text: a family tree, a lament, a parable, a law… Each passage belongs to a family (narrative, poetry, law, wisdom, prophecy, apocalyptic, letter), and often to a specific form within it.
layers.implications: Forms follow conventions. Knowing the form tells you which features are standard and which stand out, which is often where the meaning is.

layers.name: Outline
layers.description: Book outlines and sections (unfoldingWord book introductions)

categories.label: section
categories.about: A section of the book outline.
categories.implications: Shows what belongs together.

categories.label: division
categories.about: A larger division of the book.
categories.implications: Shows how the book is built.

ai_suggest.instruction: Propose literary patterns (chiasm, inclusio, parallel panels) held by a published scholar.

layers.about: How the book and passage are divided into sections and larger parts.
layers.implications: Seeing where a section starts and ends shows what belongs together and how an argument or story develops.

layers.name: Who is speaking
layers.description: Narrator and direct speech: who is speaking, quotations and asides

categories.label: speaker
categories.about: Who is speaking in this verse (found by a rule from quotation marks and speech verbs).
categories.implications: Whose words these are matters: a promise from God, a character’s claim and a crowd’s cry carry different weight.

categories.label: direct speech
categories.about: Direct speech begins here (marked in unfoldingWord’s notes).
categories.implications: Separates what characters say from the narrator’s report.

categories.label: narrator’s aside
categories.about: The narrator steps out of the story to explain background.
categories.implications: Asides show what the writer thought readers needed to know, often about customs, names or later events.

categories.label: messenger formula
categories.about: "Thus says the LORD": the messenger formula of prophetic speech.
categories.implications: Form criticism (e.g. Westermann) reads it as the convention of a royal messenger. Readings differ: a direct divine message, a prophetic convention, or both. It frames what follows as carrying the sender’s authority.

categories.label: narrative speech formula
categories.about: "And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying": divine speech framed in the third person by a narrator.
categories.implications: Readings differ: a report of actual communication; a literary and theological convention presenting law as God’s word; or a marker of a source or editorial layer. Each changes how the speech is heard.

categories.label: word-event formula
categories.about: "The word of the LORD came to…": the claim that a prophet received revelation.
categories.implications: It marks the authority claimed for what follows and often opens a book or section.

categories.label: source voice (contested)
categories.about: A proposed source voice in the Pentateuch (Priestly, Yahwist, Elohist, Deuteronomic, Holiness).
categories.implications: Always contested: shown beside traditional authorship and other models. Different authorship models change which emphases and repetitions seem significant.

layers.about: Who is speaking and how speech is framed: narrator, characters, God, prophets, speech formulas and proposed sources.
layers.implications: Whose words these are matters: a promise from God, a character’s claim and a narrator’s comment carry different weight. Formulas like "Thus says the LORD" are read in different ways, which the layer explains.
layers.caution: Source voices (Priestly, Yahwist and others) are a contested scholarly model and are always shown with the alternatives.

ai_suggest.instruction: Identify who is speaking in direct speech and where narration resumes, only where the text itself makes the speaker clear. Do not assign source-critical authors.

layers.name: Poetry & sound

categories.label: parallelism
categories.about: Parallel lines (noted by unfoldingWord).
categories.implications: The second line usually develops the first.

categories.label: poetic lines
categories.about: Verses set as poetry, with line counts.
categories.implications: Read line by line.

categories.label: acrostic
categories.about: An alphabetic acrostic: lines or stanzas start with successive Hebrew letters.
categories.implications: Signals completeness, "A to Z"; not visible in translation.

layers.about: How the text is set as poetry: lines, parallelism and acrostics.
layers.implications: Hebrew poetry works by pairing lines. Reading the second line as developing the first, not repeating it, often unlocks the meaning.

ai_suggest.instruction: Identify parallelism and poetic lines the existing tags miss. Tag acrostics only where they are well established in the Hebrew text.

categories.about: Figure of speech family: figure (general).
categories.implications: Not meant literally; recognising it shows how the writer persuades or moves the reader.

layers.about: Figures of speech (metaphor, exaggeration, rhetorical questions and more) and the families of images they use (shepherd, light, water, refuge…), from unfoldingWord Translation Notes.
layers.implications: Figures are not meant literally. Spotting one prevents an over-literal reading, and an image family links a passage to others that use the same picture.

layers.name: Themes

categories.label: theme
categories.about: A topic from Nave’s Topical Bible.
categories.implications: An index to related passages, not a claim about the main point.

layers.about: Topics and recurring motifs (from Nave’s Topical Bible).
layers.implications: Themes connect a passage to the rest of the Bible. They are a reader’s index, not a claim about the author’s main point.

layers.name: Translation lens

categories.label: translation
categories.about: A note on how this passage is translated.
categories.implications: Compare translations where it matters.

layers.about: How the stored translations render this passage, and words the translators supplied.
layers.implications: Every translation makes choices. Comparing them shows where the original is ambiguous or difficult.

layers.name: Names
layers.description: People named in each verse (Theographic) and speakers found by rule

categories.label: name
categories.about: A person named in this verse (Theographic).
categories.implications: Follow a person through the Bible.

layers.about: People and places named in each verse.
layers.implications: Names identify who is involved and often carry meaning in themselves.

layers.name: Syntax & discourse

categories.label: clause
categories.about: A clause or discourse unit.
categories.implications: Shows how sentences are built and linked.

layers.about: Clause structure and discourse connectors.
layers.implications: Connectors such as "for", "therefore" and "but" show how ideas relate. They are easy to miss in translation.

layers.name: Grammar

categories.label: morphology
categories.about: Parsed verbs (STEPBible TAHOT).
categories.implications: Verb forms carry nuance that translations can hide.

layers.about: Each verb parsed: stem, form, person, gender and number (Hebrew and Aramaic).
layers.implications: Verb forms carry nuance English can hide, for example a narrative sequence (wayyiqtol), an imperative, or an intensive stem.

layers.name: Concordance

categories.label: occurrence
categories.about: A rare word or a word count.
categories.implications: Rare words draw attention.

layers.about: How often and where each original word occurs, including rare words.
layers.implications: A rare word draws attention. A common word used in a new way may carry weight. Following a word through the Bible shows its range of meaning.

layers.name: Original words

categories.label: lemma
categories.about: The original-language text with glosses.
categories.implications: Read behind the translation.

layers.about: The original-language text (Hebrew, Aramaic or Greek) with transliteration and glosses.
layers.implications: Reading behind the translation shows wordplay, repetition and ambiguity that translations smooth over.

layers.name: Manuscripts

categories.label: variant
categories.about: A textual variant or ketiv/qere reading.
categories.implications: The readings are shown without ranking.

layers.about: Places where manuscripts or traditions differ, such as the Masoretic written-versus-read readings (ketiv/qere) or a disputed ending.
layers.implications: The text has a history of copying. Variants are usually small, but some affect meaning. They are shown without ranking.

groups.name: How people read it
groups.description: What this passage is taken to be and mean, by tradition and by scholars. Where readers disagree, every reading is shown with its source.

groups.name: The world of the text
groups.description: Places, plants and animals, everyday objects, archaeology and historical setting.

groups.name: How it’s written
groups.description: What you can see in the writing itself: its form, how it is built, who is speaking, its sound, its pictures and its themes.
